title: tenant-sla-decomposition-and-resilience-profiling-playbook
author: Maya Chen
content:
Overview

This playbook describes a pragmatic approach to decomposing customer-facing SLAs into measurable component-level SLOs for Redwood Private deployments, and a resilience profiling process that operators and SREs can run during onboarding, capacity planning, and major upgrades. It targets multi-tenant VPC and air-gapped on-prem installations where tenant isolation, predictable latency, and cost containment are primary concerns.

Goals
- Convert business SLAs (uptime, p99 latency, throughput) into component SLOs.
- Produce a resilience profile per tenant that identifies dominant failure modes and right-sized guardrails.
- Provide a reproducible test and remediation runbook for operators and field engineers.
- Ensure rollback and fallback policies are covered by SLA mapping.

Scope and assumptions
- Applies to Redwood Private (VPC and on-prem) installations where tenants are mapped to virtual deployment namespaces.
- Assumes standard Redwood runtime components (edge-gateway, tenant-router, model-service, kv-cache, routing-orchestrator) and standard observability stack (metrics: Prometheus; traces: Jaeger/OpenTelemetry; logs: central ELK/Cloud logging).
- Not a workload-specific guide; replace workload-specific thresholds (sequence length, token rate, concurrency) with tenant-specific profiling values gathered during onboarding.

Key terms
- Business SLA: commitment to the customer (e.g., "99.95% success and p99 inference latency < 250ms for <=512 tokens").
- Component SLO: internal target for a single subsystem (e.g., model-service p99 < 120ms).
- Resilience profile: summary of how a tenant’s workload reacts to component degradation (latency vs. throughput curves, cold-start sensitivity, cache-hit dependence).

Owner and escalation
- Playbook owner: Runtime Resilience Team (runtime-resilience@redwood.internal).
- Day-2 ops owner: Private Deployments Field Ops (pd-field-ops@redwood.internal).
- Oncall escalation: see /confluence/eng-sre/oncall-and-incident-response/incident-process.

SLA decomposition pattern (high level)
1. Capture the business SLA: uptime, latency bounds (p50/p95/p99), throughput or concurrency caps, and any region/residency constraints.
2. Identify critical request path and map to components: ingress -> edge-gateway -> tenant-router -> model-service -> kv-cache (optional) -> tokenizer -> response aggregation.
3. Assign per-component SLOs using conservative headroom (recommended: business p99 * 0.5 for model-stage components; see table below).
4. Define error budgets and automated fallback policies for each SLO.
5. Validate decomposition via synthetic and recorded-replay profiling under representative load.

Recommended SLO decomposition table (example)
- Business SLA: p99 inference latency < 250ms for <=512 tokens.

| Component | Example SLO | Rationale / Notes | Owner |
|---|---:|---|---|
| edge-gateway (ingress & TLS) | p99 < 30ms | Termination and rate-limiting; must be small fraction | infra-sre |
| tenant-router (routing + auth) | p99 < 20ms | Route selection + tenant ACL checks | runtime-team |
| model-service (GPU infer) | p99 < 150ms | Bulk of token generation; scale horizontally | runtime-team |
| kv-cache (prefix/KV caching) | p99 < 10ms (cache hit) | Cache hits significantly reduce model work | runtime-team |
| tokenizer / postproc | p99 < 15ms | CPU-bound transforms | infra-sre |
| network (inter-host) | p99 < 20ms | Inter-node RPCs; depends on placement | infra-network |

Notes on headroom: choose component targets so their sum + inter-component overhead <= business SLA. For high-variance workloads (long tails), increase model-service headroom or enable micro-batching to reduce variance.

Resilience profiling procedure (runbook)
1. Prepare: ensure the tenant has a representative prompt set and traffic profile. Collect: typical sequence length distribution, top-k model variants, per-call token counts, burst patterns.
2. Baseline capture (no fault): run 30-minute steady-state load at 100% of expected normal concurrency; collect p50/p95/p99, error rates, CPU/GPU utilization, KV cache hit rate.
3. Stress steps (progressive):
   a. Increase concurrency to 1.5x and 2x normal; observe latency and error rates.
   b. Introduce synthetic network latency of +10ms/+25ms on inter-host links; observe impact on p99.
   c. Drop KV cache hit ratio by simulating cache cold starts (evict and prime); measure additional latency.
   d. Simulate model-service CPU/GPU slowdowns: cap GPU frequency or inject per-call CPU delay.
   e. Toggle quantization fallback (if tenant uses multiple quantized variants) to measure quality-latency tradeoff.
4. Canary failure modes: incrementally kill 1/3 of model-service replicas and observe graceful degradation and autoscale behavior.
5. Regression validation: replay recorded traffic through a candidate upgrade in an isolated canary to assert SLO adherence.

Data to collect during profiling
- Metrics: per-component latency histograms, per-replica CPU/GPU utilization, queue depth, request-failure-type breakdown.
- Traces: end-to-end traces that can be filtered by tenant-id and operation-id.
- Artifacts: sample request/response pairs, cache hit logs, model logits for quality regressions.

Resilience profile output (artifact)
- A one-page summary that includes:
  - Tenant ID and workload class (interactive, batch, batched-interactive).
  - Baseline SLO attainment and error budget consumption.
  - Dominant failure modes (e.g., cache cold-start, model-service tail, network contention).
  - Recommended mitigations (config knobs and infra changes).
  - Risk level (Low / Medium / High) and suggested guardrail adjustments.

Mitigations catalog (examples)
- KV cache: increase memory allocation for tenant namespace; enable persistent warming pool; set cold-start TTLs.
- Model-service: pre-warm model instances for high-SLA tenants; reduce batch sizes to lower p99 at cost of throughput; set instance affinity to reduce inter-host network hops.
- Edge-gateway: add request coalescing for identical warm prefixes; tune rate limits for bursty clients.
- Autoscaler: lower decision window to respond faster for high-burst tenants; tie burst capacity to committed reserved capacity where available.

SLA-aware rollout and rollback steps (upgrade path)
1. Pre-upgrade profiling: capture resilience profile for production tenant traffic.
2. Offline regression harness: run upgrade image in isolated lab with replay of captured traffic for 2x normal concurrency for 1 hour.
3. Staged canary: deploy to 5% of capacity (non-reserved), run production traffic routing for 30–60 minutes while monitoring SLO signals and error budgets.
4. If any of these trip:
   a. Automatically route affected traffic to compatible lower-cost model variant (if configured) or to dedicated reserved pool.
   b. Trigger rollback if p99 exceeds business SLA by >25% for 10 consecutive minutes or error rate spike > 2x baseline for 5 minutes.
5. Post-rollback: preserve traces/logs and attach to incident record; run targeted profiling to find root cause.

Runbook checks and alarms (SLO guardrails)
- Alerts to fire:
  - model-service_p99 > configured-component-slo * 1.5 for 5 minutes -> P1 to runtime oncall.
  - end-to-end_p99 > business-sla * 1.25 for 10 minutes -> P0 escalation and automatic traffic fallbacks.
  - KV-cache_hit_ratio < baseline * 0.6 for 10 minutes -> P2 with automated warming job queued.
- Automated responses: scale-up policy, traffic-steer to regional fallback, enable temporary batching-mode for throughput protection.

Configuration checklist (recommended defaults)
| Config | Recommended default | Notes |
|---|---:|---|
| model-service_min_replicas | 3 | Keep >=3 for shardable stateful models to survive single-node loss |
| model-service_target_cpu_util | 60% | Tune down for low-latency tenants |
| kv-cache_initial_size_mb | 1024 | Increase for high-throughput tenants |
| autoscaler_evaluation_window_secs | 30 | Short windows for bursty interactive workloads |
| edge_gateway_rate_limit_burst | 200 | Per-tenant token bucket burst cap |

Tenant onboarding checklist (profiling-driven)
1. Collect sample traffic and run baseline profiling.
2. Generate resilience profile and map to business SLA.
3. Apply tuned component SLOs into tenant config (via control-plane API).
4. Configure alarms and automated fallbacks in console (see Redwood Console -> tenant <id> -> Guardrails).
5. Schedule periodic re-profiling (quarterly or after major workload changes).

Templates and artifacts
- Resilience profile template (copy into customer ticket): include baseline metrics chart, failure-mode heatmap, and mitigation table.
- Canary gating checklist: automated tests (latency regression, quality regression using stored prompts), manual signoff owners.
- Incident attachment template: include replay inputs, delta in cache-hit ratio, and model logits for top 10 failing examples.

Operational notes and gotchas
- Quantization fallbacks can change quality; always attach model-eval prompts to canary run to detect subtle output regressions.
- For air-gapped sites, ensure reroute policies consider limited fallback capacity and longer lead time for manual remediation.
- Reserved capacity tenants: align autoscaler policies to not evict reserved pool during multi-tenant pressure.

References

- Observability configuration standards: /confluence/architecture-and-standards/observability-standards

Appendix: example CLI commands
- Run synthetic baseline: 
  rdw-infer-bench --tenant-id tenant-123 --concurrency 50 --duration 1800 --profile-out tenant-123-baseline.json
- Deploy canary and route 5% traffic: 
  rdw-deploy canary --image v2026-03-01 --namespace tenant-123-canary
  rdw-traffic-route set --tenant tenant-123 --percent-canary 5
